en: The Scripture on the Tathāgata’s Adorned Radiance of Wisdom Entering the Realm of All Buddhas, Volume One.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmaruci of India during the Northern Wei Dynasty.

Thus have I heard: At one time the Bhagavān was dwelling on Vulture Peak Mountain in the city of Rājagṛha, within the Dharma-realm Treasury Palace on the fourth terrace, together with a great assembly of twenty thousand and fifty bhikṣus. All were arhats whose outflows were exhausted, free from further afflictions, having attained mastery over their minds; they were well-liberated in mind and well-liberated through wisdom. Their minds were thoroughly tamed; they were great dragons among men. They had done what was to be done and accomplished their task; they were freed from heavy burdens and had attained their own benefit. Having exhausted the fetters of existence, they had well-attained right knowledge. Their minds were liberated from all things and they had attained mastery, reaching the supreme further shore.
Furthermore, there were eight great śrāvakas, headed by Ājñātakauṇḍinya and others.
There were also seventy-two billion nayutas of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, whose names were:

the bodhisattva-mahāsattva Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva Sudhana-guṇa, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva Buddhavara-guṇa, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyarāja, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyasamudgata, and so forth.

All of them abide on the stage of non-retrogression and turn the great wheel of Dharma; they are skillfully able to inquire about the *Mahāvaipulya Ratnakūṭa* Dharma-gate. Their rank is that of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), having reached the ultimate Cloud of Dharma (*dharmamegha*). Their wisdom is as lofty and vast as Mount Sumeru; they have well cultivated emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*), such that no signs arise in their minds. They have all attained the most profound Dharma and the light of wisdom, and have fully accomplished the majestic deportment and conduct of a Buddha.

This assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas has all been empowered by the spiritual authority of the Buddhas; they have come from hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of Buddha-worlds in other directions, and all have attained mastery in the activities of the various supernormal powers and abide securely within the reality-limit of the dharma-nature.
At that time, the World-Honored One had this thought:

"I shall now turn the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma, desiring to cause all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas to swiftly give rise to the power of great wisdom, and further desiring to cause bodhisattvas of great majesty and great supernormal powers from worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges to assemble here."
At that time, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, again thought to himself:
"I shall preach the Dharma-gate of the Great Vaipulya and wish to manifest auspicious signs by emitting great radiance.
For what reason?"
"I wish to cause all the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have come here to inquire about the Dharma I am teaching.

At that time, having thought this, the World-Honored One emitted a great cloud of light that universally illuminated worlds throughout the ten directions as numerous as the atoms in incalculable, inconceivable trichiliocosms.

Immediately, from each of the worlds in the ten directions, there arrived and gathered together bodhisattva-mahāsattvas equal in number to the atoms within ten times ten incalculable buddha-lands, hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of nayutas.
Each and every bodhisattva, by means of their respective bodhisattva supernormal powers, offered all manner of inconceivable and most supreme offerings to the Buddhas.

Each of those bodhisattvas, by the power of their respective original vows, ascended lotus seats before the Tathāgata; with single-minded devotion they contemplated the Buddha, gazing up at him as they remained there.

At that moment, from within the Palace of the Dharma-realm Treasury, a great precious lotus-treasury high seat sprang forth from the earth, measuring one hundred million nayutas of asankhyeyas of yojanas in length and breadth.

The form and appearance of these flowers were perfectly proportioned from top to bottom. They were composed of *maṇi* jewels of universal radiance; they had railings all around made of *maṇi* jewels of lightning-like brilliance; their stalks were made of *maṇi* jewels of inconceivable radiance; they were accompanied by retinues of inconceivable *maṇi* jewels; they had hanging tassels made of *maṇi* jewels of radiance surpassing all metaphors; they had nets made of *maṇi* jewels of sovereign kings; they were interspersed with various kinds of *maṇi* jewels; and they suspended immeasurable jeweled canopies, banners, and streamers.
That great jewel lotus-treasury high seat radiated ten *asaṃkhyeya* hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of *nayuta* rays of light from its circumference.

At that time, these lights shone everywhere throughout immeasurable worlds in the ten directions. Immediately, in each of the ten directions, there were ten billion unspeakable numbers of Buddha-lands, where devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, the four great heavenly kings, Śakra Devendra, Brahmā Devarāja, and others—equal in number to the atoms within hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of *nayutas*—all came together for the assembly.

Those devas each mounted their own precious palaces and towers; every one of them was accompanied by inconceivable, asankhyeya numbers of celestial maidens who performed hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of various musical performances for their entertainment, as they arrived at the place where the Buddha was.
Furthermore, there were various devas, nāgas, and others, each riding upon flower-palaces and multi-storied towers, who came to where the Buddha was.
Again, there were various devas, nāgas, and others, each riding upon sandalwood palaces and multi-storied towers made of uragasāra sandalwood, who came to where the Buddha was.
Furthermore, there were various devas, nāgas, and others, each riding upon palatial towers and pavilions made of genuine jewels, who came to where the Buddha was.
Moreover, there were various devas, nāgas, and others, each riding upon palatial towers and pavilions of various colors, who came to where the Buddha was.
Furthermore, there were various devas, nāgas, and others, each riding upon a jeweled palace and pavilion of *vajra-prabhāsa-maṇi-ratna*, coming to where the Buddha was.
Again, there were various devas, nāgas, and others, each riding upon a jeweled palace and pavilion of *jambūnada-suvarṇa*, coming to where the Buddha was.
Furthermore, there were various devas, nāgas, and others, each riding upon palatial towers made of *maṇi* jewels that gather all radiance, coming to the place where the Buddha was.
Furthermore, there were various devas, nāgas, and others, each riding upon palatial towers made of *maṇi* jewels of the Sovereign King (*Vaiśrāvaṇa-rāja*), coming to the place where the Buddha was.
Furthermore, there were various devas, nāgas, and others, each riding upon palatial towers made of wish-fulfilling maṇi jewels, coming to where the Buddha was.
Moreover, there were various devas, nāgas, and others, each riding upon palatial towers made of maṇi jewels from the necklaces worn beneath the necks of King Śakra, coming to where the Buddha was.

Furthermore, there were various devas, nāgas, and others, each riding upon and upholding palatial towers made of great maṇi-jewels that emit a thousand rays of light from the pure great ocean, as they came to the place where the Buddha was.

Each of these groups was accompanied by an inconceivable number of asaṃkhyeya celestial maidens, who performed hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nāyutas of various musical performances for their entertainment as they arrived at the place where the Buddha was.
Having arrived, they together performed various kinds of music—transcending all worlds, inconceivable, incomparable, immeasurable, and incalculable—to make offerings to the Tathāgata.

By the power of their original vows, those devas had all their needs for the seats spontaneously fulfilled; they withdrew to sit to one side and remained there, gazing up at the Buddha with a sincere mind.

At that time, the great earth of the trichiliocosm became Jāmbūnada gold. The world was adorned with various mani-jewel trees, various celestial flower trees, various clothing trees, various uragasāra sandalwood trees, and various incense trees. Nets made of lightning-flash mani-jewels covered the entire trichiliocosm, and great precious banners were erected, with various streamers and canopies suspended from them.

Within each of those trees, there were hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of asankhyeyas of celestial maidens, all manifesting half their bodies, holding in both hands hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of various precious necklaces, remaining there in worship.
At that time, from within that great precious lotus-treasury lion throne, a wondrous sound emerged and spoke these verses:
“I have been born through the power of the Buddha; My original vow is now fulfilled.
I pray that the King of Men will come and sit here, To honor and support the Honored One among Two-Legged Beings.”
This body of mine is composed solely of jewels, pure as a flower and desired by all;
its formation through the power of the Buddha, may the Honored One fulfill my vow:
sitting upon the Lion-Flower Treasury, may you adorn the world and me.
The Dharma has been preached and heard by many; you have attained the lion’s throne.
My body emits a thousand rays of light that illuminate immeasurable worlds;
I pray that the Honored One will sit upon me, giving rise to a heart of joy within me.
"In this place where the Dharma is taught, eight hundred million Buddhas have already sat;
may the World-Honored One now sit swiftly, to gather us in and benefit us.

At that time, the World-Honored One rose from his original seat, ascended the great precious lotus-treasury lion throne, and sat cross-legged. He surveyed the assembly of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, and desiring to preach the supreme and wondrous Dharma for the sake of the bodhisattvas, he immediately manifested a sign.
At that moment, the entire assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas had this thought:

"The Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī should inquire of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, concerning the dharma-gate of non-arising and non-ceasing, for we have already heard this supreme and wondrous dharma-gate since long ago."
At that time, the Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī, having observed the signs of the Tathāgata and knowing the thoughts in the minds of the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"What dharma-gate is called 'neither arising nor ceasing'?
He then spoke this verse:
"The Buddha speaks of non-arising and non-ceasing; what characteristics does he explain therein?"
Which phenomena are neither born nor extinguished?
I pray you, explain this with appropriate metaphors.
For the sake of wisdom, the Bodhisattvas, sustained by the spiritual power of all Buddhas, [inquire].
"Come from immeasurable worlds; we pray that you will preach the supreme and wondrous Dharma.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
Mañjuśrī! You are able to ask the Buddha about this most profound meaning. Mañjuśrī!

You act for the peace and security of immeasurable sentient beings; you are able to bestow various kinds of happiness upon immeasurable sentient beings; furthermore, you are able to have compassion for immeasurable sentient beings, extensively benefit immeasurable sentient beings, grant the bliss of humans and devas to immeasurable sentient beings, and serve as the ultimate ground of Buddhahood for all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
Mañjuśrī! Do not be startled or terrified by this meaning. Mañjuśrī!
I shall teach you the dharma of non-arising and non-ceasing; you should rely upon wisdom for its understanding. Mañjuśrī!
That which is the dharma of non-arising and non-ceasing is precisely the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
“Mañjuśrī! It is as if the great earth were composed of great lapis lazuli, its form and appearance being just like the dwelling place of the Trāyastriṃśa gods.”

Within that great earth, one clearly perceives the reflection of Śakra, the Lord of the Thirty-three Heavens, together with the Sudharmā Hall; furthermore, one sees all the fivefold sensual pleasures and the various delights and amusements belonging to the celestial realm of the divine king Śakra—all of these are seen.
At that time, the devas proclaimed to all men, women, boys, and girls, saying:

"Come, you may come to behold this Hall of Good Dharma of Śakra Devānām Indra, King of Gods, as well as the fivefold sensual realms and the implements for play and delight belonging to the King of Gods."
He further spoke these words:
"O sons and daughters of good family! You should practice giving, maintain the precepts, and plant various roots of goodness;

you shall all obtain this Hall of Good Dharma and the fivefold sensual pleasures of the heavens, as well as the implements for play and delight. You shall become heavenly kings and, together with their karmic rewards and supernormal powers, will—just like Śakra Devānām Indra—ultimately achieve and surely enjoy whatever sensory realms they possess."

“Mañjuśrī! At that time, those sons and daughters of good family, as well as the youths and maidens, saw within that great lapis lazuli ground the clear reflection of the Hall of Good Dharma (Sudharmā) of Śakra, Lord of the Thirty-three Heavens, along with the realms of the five desires and the implements for play and pleasure. They immediately scattered flowers and, with palms joined in worship, spoke these words:
‘Just as this body of Śakra, Lord of the Thirty-three, as well as the Hall of Good Dharma and the realms of the five desires in that heaven, may we also obtain them.’”

"Mañjuśrī! Those sentient beings are entirely unaware of such matters as the Hall of Good Dharma in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, Śakra Devānām Indra, and the realm of the five desires; all of these appear within the ground of great vaidūrya."
Why is this? Because the ground of great vaidūrya is pure, all reflections appear within it. Mañjuśrī!

Furthermore, those sentient beings, seeking the body of Śakra, the Heavenly King, dedicate all their practices of giving, observance of precepts, and cultivation of various roots of goodness toward rebirth in the Heaven of the Thirty-three.

Mañjuśrī! In reality, within the ground of great vaidūrya, there are no such things as the Sudharmā Hall of the Trāyastriṃśa gods, Śakra Devānām Indra, or the realms of the five desires; it is only because the ground of great vaidūrya jewel is so pure that their reflected images appear.

That Hall of Good Dharma in the Heaven of the Thirty-three, and the realm of the five desires of Śakra Devānām-indra, do not arise and do not cease because they are unreal; they appear as pure mirror-images upon the ground of great vaidūrya jewel.
“Mañjuśrī! It is so, it is so.
All sentient beings, by practicing according to reality based upon their pure minds, perceive the body of the Tathāgata, Mañjuśrī!”
All sentient beings perceive the body of the Tathāgata by relying on the power of the Tathāgata’s empowerment.

Yet the body of the Tathāgata is not substantial; it is neither born nor extinguished, neither a thing nor a non-thing, neither visible nor invisible, neither observable nor unobservable, neither possessing mind nor devoid of mind, neither conceivable nor inconceivable, and neither existent nor non-existent.

“Mañjuśrī! All sentient beings, by virtue of the power of the mirror-like reflection of the Tathāgata’s pure Dharma-body, are able to see the Tathāgata’s pure Dharma-body. They offer precious robes, scatter flowers, burn incense, join their palms in worship, and speak these words:
‘I, too, shall attain the pure Dharma-body of a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.’”

"Mañjuśrī! All those sentient beings, seeking the Tathāgata’s pure Dharma-body, practice giving, uphold the precepts, and plant various roots of goodness; by means of these roots of goodness, they seek the wisdom of the Tathāgata and dedicate them toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."

“Mañjuśrī! Just as the body of Śakra, King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, within the mirror-image of that great Vaiḍūrya ground is unmoving and unarisen; its mind is free from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), non-discriminating, and does not discriminate or even non-discriminate; it is without thought, without thinking, inconceivable, and without recollection; it is quiescent and tranquil, neither arising nor ceasing; it cannot be seen, heard, smelled, tasted, or touched; it is devoid of all marks (*lakṣaṇa*), and is neither perceivable nor cognizable.

In this way, Mañjuśrī! The pure *dharmakāya* of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, is likewise: unmoving and unarisen; its mind is free from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), free from discrimination, neither discriminating nor non-discriminating; it is without thought and without thinking, inconceivable and without recollection; it is quiescent and tranquil, neither arising nor ceasing; it cannot be seen, heard, smelled, tasted, or touched; it is devoid of all marks (*lakṣaṇa*), and is neither perceivable nor cognizable.
“Mañjuśrī! The Dharma-body of the Tathāgata is neither born nor extinguished; it neither departs nor arrives, taking this as its essence, like a reflection in a mirror.”
As perceived by the world, the Tathāgata manifests various different bodies according to the diverse powers of faith of sentient beings;
according to the length of the response from those sentient beings, the life-span of the manifested body of the Tathāgata is long or short;
and according to the power of faith they have regarding great enlightenment, the Tathāgata manifests his body.
The Tathāgata manifests his body according to those sentient beings who, upon hearing the Dharma, are able to believe and accept it;
he manifests his body according to those sentient beings whose faith enables them to understand the teachings of the Three Vehicles;
and he manifests his body according to those sentient beings who attain the power of liberation.

“Mañjuśrī! For example, in the void there is a great and wondrous Dharma-drum, produced by the power of the merits of the Trāyastriṃśa gods. It is detached from the Sudharmā Hall and resides in the midst of space, beyond the range of the visual and cognitive faculties of all the devas; it cannot be seen and cannot be observed.”
Mañjuśrī! At what time does that great and wondrous Dharma drum emit its sound? Mañjuśrī!

Because those devas are addicted to the objects of the five desires and never abandon them, their heedlessness increases; they do not enter the Hall of Good Dharma to hear the teachings and contemplate their meaning.

Śakra Devānām Indra was likewise addicted to the realm of the five desires and never ceased from them; his negligence increased, and he did not enter the Hall of Good Dharma nor ascend the high seat to preach the Dharma to the devas.
At that time, that great and wondrous Dharma drum—invisible, unobservable, and beyond the range of the eye—resided in the midst of space and emitted the sound of the sublime Dharma.
The sound of that sublime Dharma resounded throughout the Heaven of the Thirty-three, and it spoke these words:
"O devas, you should know that all forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects are entirely impermanent; do not practice heedlessness, for the rewards of heaven swiftly decline."
"O devas, you should know that all conditioned phenomena are suffering, all conditioned phenomena are empty, and all conditioned phenomena are without self.
Therefore, O devas, do not practice heedlessness."
If one falls away from celestial retribution and is born in another place of suffering,
the devas should together deliberate upon the Dharma, delight in the Dharma, rejoice in the Dharma, savor the Dharma, accord with the Dharma, and remain mindful of the Dharma.
"If the devas wish not to abandon their celestial retribution and the realms of the five desires, they should practice correctly.

"Mañjuśrī! That sound of the Dharma drum is invisible and formless; it is non-conceptual and without discrimination; it transcends the realm of the eye; it is neither born nor extinguished; it is free from sound and speech; and it is detached from mind, thought, and consciousness."

Mañjuśrī! At that time, when the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven heard the sound of the wondrous drum, they immediately entered the Sudharmā Hall to deliberate upon the Dharma, delight in the Dharma, rejoice in the Dharma, savor the Dharma, accord with the Dharma, and mindfully contemplate the Dharma, practicing according to what has been taught.
When he passes away from that heaven, he is reborn in another superior realm.
Śakra Devānām Indra likewise enters the Hall of Good Dharma, ascends the high Dharma seat, and preaches the Dharma for the sake of the devas.

“Mañjuśrī! When the asuras engage in battle with those devas of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven and the Trāyastriṃśa devas are weak in strength and retreat, at that time the Dharma drum produces such a sound in the midst of the void;
hearing it, the asuras are struck with great terror and withdraw into the great ocean.”

"Mañjuśrī! That great Dharma drum has no form or characteristics and no creator; it cannot be seen or observed. It is fundamentally without reality and is inconceivable; it is without mind and without marks, without color and without sound, without substance and without duality, transcending the realm of the eye."

Mañjuśrī! Based on their past karma, that great and wondrous drum produces sounds in the sky, causing those devas to remain far removed from all obstacles and afflictions, free from defilement, and tranquil.

“Mañjuśrī! Just as that great Dharma drum in the sky is invisible and cannot be observed, fundamentally non-substantial and inconceivable, without mind and without marks, without form and without sound, without substance and without duality, transcending the realm of the eye—yet by virtue of its original karma, the Dharma drum produces a sound that causes the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to remain far removed from all obstructions, sorrows, and afflictions, becoming untainted and tranquil.”

Mañjuśrī! Just as when the minds of the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven become heedless, that sublime Dharma drum emits a great sound, causing the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven to distance themselves from all obstacles and afflictions, becoming untainted and tranquil.

“Mañjuśrī! Thus, the pure *dharmakāya* of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, cannot be seen by any in the world; it is fundamentally without reality and inconceivable, without mind and without marks, without form, without substance, and without duality, transcending the sphere of the eye.”

Mañjuśrī! Just as those sentient beings, depending on their fundamental karmic actions, are able to hear the sound of the Dharma according to what their minds can believe, so too does that sound of the Dharma enable sentient beings to distance themselves from all obstacles and afflictions, becoming undefiled and tranquil.

Mañjuśrī! That pure dharmakāya is without speech and without substance; yet, by the power of their roots of goodness and karma, sentient beings hear the sound of the sublime Dharma, thinking, "The Tathāgata is preaching the Dharma," and "There is a Buddha in the world."

Mañjuśrī! When all sentient beings hear the voice of the Tathāgata, they are able to obtain all requisites of happiness; those who have already developed faith are led to attain correct understanding. This correct understanding upon hearing the voice is the body of the Tathāgata.

Bodhisattvas who have first resolved their minds toward enlightenment, as well as all ordinary sentient beings, hear the Tathāgata preach the Dharma and contemplate the Tathāgata, thereby increasing all their roots of goodness.
“Mañjuśrī! The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha’s pure Dharma-body is neither born nor extinguished; it should be understood in this way. Mañjuśrī!”

For example, in early summer, by the power of the fundamental karma of all sentient beings, all seeds, grains, grasses, forests, medicinal herbs, and trees upon the great earth sprout and grow, serving as the means for the livelihood and happiness of sentient beings.
From the upper reaches of space, such winds emerge; these winds are able to produce great clouds;
the production of great clouds is able to pour down heavy rain;
the pouring down of heavy rain is able to fill the great earth.
That which fills the great earth enables all seeds to flourish.
At that time, all the people of Jambudvīpa were filled with great joy and leaped for joy, saying:
"This is a great cloud! This is a great rain!"
"Mañjuśrī! When the heavens do not send rain in the sky, the people of Jambudvīpa say:
'There are no clouds; there is no rain.'"
"Mañjuśrī! Whenever great clouds arise everywhere and heavy rain falls universally, all sentient beings will say:
'How rare is this great cloud!'"
"How rare is this great rain!
It pours down everywhere, filling the great earth.
Thus it was said, Mañjuśrī!
Yet that space is without clouds and without rain.
Mañjuśrī! Depending upon and caused by the wind, those great clouds can arise and that great rain can fall within that space.
Mañjuśrī! Depending upon and caused by wind, there is neither cloud nor rain in that space. Why is this?
This is because it depends upon the power of the fundamental karma of sentient beings. "Mañjuśrī!
Just as that mass of water gathers in the midst of space and remains there through the conditions of the wind, raining down in dependence upon the wind, yet people of the world call it 'cloud-rain'."
Why is this? It is because, by the power of the fundamental karma of sentient beings, a great mass of rain pours down from the midst of space, filling the great earth. Mañjuśrī!
In that space above, there are no clouds and no rain. Mañjuśrī!
That great cloud-rain is by its very nature neither born nor extinguished; it is free from mind, thought, and consciousness, and free from the characteristics of going and coming.

“Mañjuśrī! In this way, all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, relying upon past roots of goodness and cultivating various virtuous practices, hear the Buddha’s teaching of the Dharma and attain the path free from obstacles;
all sentient beings, as well as all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, plant various roots of goodness and seek the path to nirvāṇa.”
The beings of the world will then say:
"The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha has appeared in the world; the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata is all true speech, speech as it is, and speech that is not otherwise."
"Moreover, O Mañjuśrī, because of the power of the roots of goodness of sentient beings,
the Dharma-body produces sound, and thus the devas and humans declare:
'The Tathāgata preaches the Dharma.'"
"Mañjuśrī! In reality, there is no Tathāgata.
Why is this? Because..."
The Dharma-body of the Tathāgata is without marks and free from marks; it is without location and free from location; it is not real, unarisen, and unceasing. Mañjuśrī!

Furthermore, that Tathāgata possesses the eloquence of joyful exposition; he teaches the Dharma to devas and humans without end, causing all who hear it according to their needs to attain understanding and liberation. "Mañjuśrī!..."

For Bodhisattvas who have first resolved their minds as well as all ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*), because of the power of the fundamental karma of sentient beings, if it is appropriate for them to see the Tathāgata enter parinirvāṇa, the Tathāgata then enters parinirvāṇa and cannot be seen.
Yet those sentient beings give rise to such a thought, saying:
"The Tathāgata has entered ultimate parinirvāṇa. Mañjuśrī!
The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, is neither born nor does he die; he neither arises nor ceases. Mañjuśrī!
Since beginningless time, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha has realized the eternally abiding Great Parinirvāṇa.

“Mañjuśrī! Just as that great cloud is unreal, unarisen, and unceasing—existing only through delusion—yet sentient beings conceive of it through mental constructs and give it the provisional names ‘cloud’ and ‘rain.’”

Mañjuśrī! The Tathāgata is unreal, unarisen, and unceasing; he is fundamentally unborn. Yet, according to the mental conceptions of sentient beings, they hear that the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, currently exists and expounds the Dharma.

“Mañjuśrī! For example, it is like the Great Sovereign Brahmā King, who exercises unimpeded mastery over ten hundred thousand myriads of trichiliocosm worlds; he looks down upon all the celestial palaces, even as far as those of the Four Heavenly Kings.”

At that time, the Great Brahmā King Maheśvara, acting as the sovereign lord over those ten hundred thousand million triple-thousand great thousandfold world systems, surveyed all the celestial palaces of the devas.

Mañjuśrī! At that time, all the devas within the palace each abandoned the objects of the five desires and all musical performances; casting aside all thoughts of sensual desire, they gave rise to a heart of great reverence, joined their palms in worship to the Great Brahmā King, and remained gazing up at him.
Mañjuśrī! That Great Lord Brahmā King appears for a brief moment within all those palaces.
At that time, the gods, in order to be born in the Brahma world, dedicate all their roots of goodness toward Brahmā.

Mañjuśrī! That Great Sovereign Brahmā, Lord of ten hundred thousand million trichiliocosms, does not fall back from the Brahma-heaven but dwells sustaining the Brahma-palace. By the power of his sovereign vows and sustaining force, and by the power of the roots of goodness of all sentient beings, he manifests as a transformed Brahmā and observes them day after day.

All the celestial palaces, down to those of the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, each abandoned the objects of the five desires and all musical performances; casting aside all thoughts of sensual craving, they gave rise to a heart of great reverence, joined their palms in worship of the Great Brahmā King, and remained gazing up at him.
Then that Great Lord Brahmā, King of the Gods, temporarily manifests his body within all those palaces without moving from his original location.
At that time, the gods, in order to be born in the Brahma world, dedicate all their roots of goodness toward the realm of Brahmā.
“Mañjuśrī! Yet, in that place, there is no real Brahmā. Mañjuśrī!”

That Brahmā-heaven is empty; that Brahmā-heaven is non-existent and unreal. It has no name and no sound; it has no dwelling place and no substance. It is inconceivable and signless, transcending mind, thought, and consciousness; it is neither born nor extinguished.

Mañjuśrī! By the power of the sustaining force of that Great Brahmā’s own original vows and roots of goodness, and by the power of the sustaining force of the roots of goodness of those various devas, he manifests his body for a brief time within all those celestial palaces.

Mañjuśrī! Those gods do not know that the body of the Brahmā-deva is empty, non-existent, and unreal; that it has no name and no sound; that it has no dwelling place and no substance; that it is inconceivable and signless; and that it is beyond mind, thought, and consciousness, being neither born nor extinguished.

"In this way, Mañjuśrī, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha is empty, non-existent, unreal; he has no name and no sound, no dwelling place and no essence; he is inconceivable and signless, transcending mind, thought, and consciousness, and is likewise neither born nor extinguished."

Mañjuśrī! The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, by means of the power of the original vows and practices of those bodhisattvas, sustains bodhisattvas who have first resolved their minds [on enlightenment], as well as all those who abide in the vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.

By the power of the roots of goodness of all ordinary worldlings, the Tathāgata manifests a body adorned with hundreds of thousands of marks and signs, like a reflection in a mirror, while remaining unmoved from its original place.

Mañjuśrī! Bodhisattvas who have first resolved their minds, all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and ordinary worldlings of the path of hair do not know that the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, is empty, non-existent, unreal, and unobservable; that he is without name, without sound, without abode, and without essence; that he is inconceivable, signless, transcends mind, thought, and consciousness, and is neither born nor extinguished.

Mañjuśrī! The Tathāgata is fully endowed with a body adorned by hundreds of thousands of millions of various marks and signs; through all his various modes of conduct and deportment, he utters a great and wondrous sound to preach the Dharma for sentient beings according to their various inclinations. He is able to cause sentient beings to distance themselves from all obstacles, anxieties, and afflictions, becoming untainted and tranquil; yet the Tathāgata’s mind of universal equanimity remains without discrimination or dualistic thought.
“Mañjuśrī! For this reason, that which is said to be neither born nor extinguished is called the Tathāgata.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
“The Tathāgata is eternally unborn, and all phenomena are likewise so;
there are no real dharmas in the world, yet the ignorant falsely grasp at signs.
Within the untainted wholesome dharmas, there is neither suchness nor a Tathāgata.”
By the power of that wholesome dharma, one appears in this present life like a reflection in a mirror.

"Mañjuśrī! It is as if, when the sun first rises, it first illuminates the greatest of mountain kings; next, it illuminates Mount Cakravāḍa and Mount Mahācakravāḍa; next, it illuminates other great mountains; next, it illuminates other dark mountains; next, it illuminates high plateaus and mounds; and finally, it illuminates deep valleys and low-lying places."
Mañjuśrī! That sunlight does not discriminate, is without discrimination, and does not engage in mental deliberation. Why is this?

Mañjuśrī! That solar radiance is without mind, thought, or consciousness; it is neither arising nor ceasing; it is signless and free from signs; it is without recollection and free from recollection; it is without conceptual proliferation, without obstruction, and free from obstructions; it does not abide on this shore nor on the other shore; it is neither high nor low; it is neither bound nor liberated; it is neither knowing nor non-knowing; it is without affliction and yet not without affliction; it is neither real nor unreal; it is not on this shore nor on the other shore; it is not on dry land nor in the water; it is not on both shores nor in the middle of the stream; it is without perception and free from perception; it is without form and yet not without form.
“Mañjuśrī! Depending upon the great earth, there are high, low, and middle [elevations], and the sunlight follows these with its own high, low, and middle [intensities]. Mañjuśrī!”
The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha is also like this: he does not discriminate, is without discrimination, and does not engage in mental deliberation. Mañjuśrī, why is this?
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is free from mind, thought, and consciousness; he is neither born nor extinguished; he is signless and free from signs;
he is without recollection and free from recollection; he is without conceptual proliferation and free from conceptual proliferation;
he is without feverish distress and free from feverish distress; he does not abide on this shore, nor does he abide on the other shore.
Neither high nor low, neither bound nor liberated, neither knowing nor not knowing,
neither afflicted nor unafflicted, neither a speaker of truth nor a speaker of untruth,
not on this shore, not on the other shore, not on dry land, and not in the water.
Neither on the two shores nor in the middle of the stream; neither one who possesses all-knowledge nor one who does not possess all-knowledge;
neither an awakened one nor one who is not awakened; neither a practitioner nor one who is not a practitioner;
neither one who cultivates nor one who does not cultivate; neither one who is mindful nor one who is not mindful. Not...
It is not one who possesses mind, nor is it one who lacks mind; it is not one who is apart from mind, nor is it one who is not apart from mind;
it is not one who lacks intention, nor is it one who lacks intention; it is not one who harms, nor is it one who does not harm; it is not one who has a name, nor is it one who has no name;
it is not one who has form, nor is it one who has no form; it is not one who speaks, nor is it one who does not speak.
The speaker is neither one who employs provisional designations nor one for whom there are no provisional designations; neither one who is visible nor one who is invisible.
Their essential nature is thus and not otherwise. They are neither one who speaks of the Path nor one for whom there is no speaking of the Path;
neither one who realizes the fruit nor one for whom there is no realization of the fruit; they do not engage in conceptual discrimination.
It is not one who lacks non-conceptualization; it is not one who is free from conceptualization; nor is it one who does not lack freedom from conceptualization. Mañjuśrī!

Just as there are superior, middling, and inferior natures among sentient beings throughout that boundless realm of phenomena, so too does the Tathāgata emit the great sun-disk of wisdom-light to universally illumine all sentient beings.

First, it illuminates the mountain kings of the Great Vehicle—the pure and straightforward minds of all bodhisattvas; next, it illuminates those who abide in the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas; next, it illuminates those who abide in the vehicle of the śrāvakas; next, it illuminates sentient beings who practice wholesome deeds according to their respective capacities for faith; and finally, it illuminates even those sentient beings who abide in the category of the wrong-natured. All are illuminated by the sun-disk of the Tathāgata’s omniscience, for the sake of ultimately benefiting all sentient beings, for the sake of producing all future roots of goodness, and for the sake of causing all roots of goodness to increase.
“Mañjuśrī! Regarding all those matters, the Tathāgata maintains a mind of equanimous relinquishment, without discrimination and without divergent thoughts. Mañjuśrī!”
The sun-disc of wisdom of all Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, has no such thought as:
"I shall preach the sublime Dharma for these sentient beings, but I shall not preach the Dharma for those sentient beings."
"Mañjuśrī! The Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, possess no such discriminating mind as to think:

'This sentient being has faith in the superior Dharma; this sentient being has faith in the middling Dharma; this sentient being has faith in the inferior Dharma; this sentient being has faith in the true Dharma; this sentient being has faith in the false Dharma.'"
"Mañjuśrī! The Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, do not harbor such thoughts as:
'This sentient being has faith in the supreme Dharma; I shall preach the Mahāyāna for them.'"
To those sentient beings who have faith in the intermediate Dharma, he teaches the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle;
to those sentient beings who have faith in the inferior Dharma, he teaches the Śrāvaka Vehicle;
to those sentient beings who have faith in right practice, he teaches the Dharma of the pure mind.
"Even unto those sentient beings who believe in false practices, he preaches the Dharma according to what they should hear. Mañjuśrī!
The sun-disk of the wisdom of all Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, possesses no such discriminating mind.
Why is this? Because the sun-disk of wisdom of all Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, is far removed from all conceptualization, discursive differentiation, and all frivolous proliferation. Mañjuśrī!
In accordance with the various roots of goodness of sentient beings, the sun-disc of the wisdom of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, appears in various distinct ways. "Mañjuśrī!

It is like a wish-fulfilling jewel within the great ocean, suspended upon a high banner; according to whatever thoughts any sentient being has and whatever things they require, they hear the sound of that maṇi jewel issuing forth in just such a way."
Yet that maṇi jewel does not discriminate, is without discrimination, and does not engage in thought; it is without mind, free from the mind, and detached from mind, intellect, and consciousness.
“Mañjuśrī! The Tathāgata is also like this: he does not discriminate, is without discrimination, and does not engage in mental reflection;
he is without mind and free from mind, detached from the mind, intellect, and consciousness; he is unfathomable and free from all measurement.”
It is immeasurable; it cannot be attained, nor is it apart from attainment. Greed cannot turn it, hatred cannot turn it, and delusion cannot turn it.
It is neither unreal nor false; it is neither permanent nor impermanent; it is neither illumination nor non-illumination;
it is neither clarity nor lack of clarity; it is neither an awakener nor a non-awakener. It is not...
Unborn and unceasing, inconceivable and beyond the reach of thought, without essence and free from essence,
neither to be grasped nor to be abandoned, beyond frivolous conceptualization, ineffable,
and transcending all verbal expression; without delight and free from delight, unborn, incalculable, and beyond all measure and number.
Non-going, without going, and the stillness of going; it cuts off all realms of existence and is free from all verbal expression;
it cannot be seen, cannot be observed, and cannot be grasped; it is neither empty nor non-empty, neither visible nor expressible, neither a combination nor separate from a combination.
It is not made, not created, and not demonstrated; it is neither defiled nor purifiable; it is neither name nor form;
it is neither with signs nor signless; it is neither karma nor the retribution of karma;
it is neither past, future, nor present; it is neither possessed of afflictions nor free from afflictions; and it is without dispute.
It is not non-contention; it is not sound, but is free from all sounds; it is wordless, signless, and free from all signs;
it is neither internal, nor external, nor even in between.

Mañjuśrī! The Tathāgata’s precious jewel of pure and straightforward mind is suspended atop the lofty banner of great compassion; according to the various kinds of faith of sentient beings and the various kinds of conduct of sentient beings, they hear the sound of the Dharma being taught in such and such ways.
Mañjuśrī! The Tathāgata maintains a mind of equanimous relinquishment toward all matters, being without discrimination and without divergent thoughts. Mañjuśrī!
For example, like an echo, which issues from another and is heard by sentient beings, that echo is neither past, nor future, nor present;
it cannot be apprehended as internal, external, or in between the two; it is neither born nor extinguished, neither annihilated nor permanent.
It is neither knowing nor not knowing; neither awakening nor not awakening;
neither clarity nor lack of clarity; neither bondage nor liberation; neither destruction nor non-destruction; neither mindfulness nor non-mindfulness;
neither abiding nor non-abiding; neither dwelling nor non-dwelling; and it is not the element of earth.
It is not the water element, not the fire element, not the wind element; it is neither conditioned nor unconditioned;
it is neither conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) nor non-proliferation; it is neither sound nor non-sound; it is neither seeing nor non-seeing;
it is neither syllables, nor speech, nor the departure from speech; it is neither measurable nor beyond measure.
It is not a measure, nor is it characterized by marks, nor is it devoid of marks; it is not quiescent, nor is it devoid of quiescence;
it is neither long nor short; it is neither mind nor non-mind; it is neither contemplation nor non-contemplation;
it is neither a visible mark nor an invisible mark; it is neither empty nor non-empty, for its own-being is empty.
It is to be contemplated, not not to be contemplated; it is free from that which is to be contemplated. It is neither to be perceived nor not to be perceived;
it is free from mind, thought, and consciousness. It is equal in all places, without discrimination, free from divergent discrimination, and transcends the three periods of time.
Mañjuśrī! That sound follows the various sentient beings, and through their various voices, they hear various echoes. Mañjuśrī!
The sound of the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, is likewise:
it is neither past, nor future, nor present; it cannot be apprehended as internal, external, or in between the two;
it is neither arising nor ceasing, neither annihilated nor eternal, and neither known nor unknown.
It is neither awakening nor non-awakening; neither clarity nor lack of clarity; neither bondage nor liberation;
neither destruction nor non-destruction; neither recollection nor non-recollection;
neither abiding nor non-abiding; neither dwelling nor non-dwelling; and it is neither the earth element, nor the water element, nor the fire element.
It is not the wind element; it is neither conditioned nor unconditioned; it is neither conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) nor non-proliferation;
it is neither sound nor non-sound; it is neither seeing nor non-seeing;
it is neither letters nor speech, yet it is not apart from speech; it is neither measurement nor apart from measurement; it is neither characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) nor apart from characteristics.
It is neither quiescent nor apart from quiescence; it is neither long nor short; it is neither mind nor non-mind;
it is neither contemplation nor non-contemplation; it is neither a visible characteristic nor an invisible characteristic;
it is neither empty nor non-empty, for its own-being is empty; it is neither conceivable nor inconceivable.
It is free from that which can be conceived; it is neither perceivable nor imperceivable. It is detached from mind, thought, and consciousness;
it is equal in all places, without discrimination, free from divergent discrimination, and transcends the three periods of time.

Mañjuśrī! According to the various inclinations and various understandings of sentient beings, they hear the sounds of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, preaching the Dharma in such and such ways.
“Mañjuśrī! It is like the great earth, which sustains all things and brings to completion and fulfillment the growth of all grains, wheat, fruits, melons, grasses, shrubs, and forests.

Mañjuśrī! That great earth does not engage in discrimination or false discrimination; it is equal in all places, without discrimination, without false discrimination, and without mind. It is free from mind, thought, and consciousness.

“Mañjuśrī! It is likewise with the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha. Relying upon the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, he sustains all sentient beings, causes all roots of goodness to grow, and establishes and brings to fruition the various roots of goodness belonging to all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and those of various heterodox views such as the Nirgranthas who follow wrong views, even down to all sentient beings in the category of the fixed in error.

All those roots of goodness are sustained by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha; they all grow, develop, and reach fulfillment in dependence upon the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.

“Mañjuśrī! The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is free from all conceptualization; he is without conceptualization, without differentiated conceptualization, and without thought. He is free from all mind, mentation, and consciousness; he is unobservable and free from all observation; he is invisible and free from all views; he is inconceivable and free from all conception; he is beyond recollection and free from all recollection. His mind is equanimous, yet there is no equanimity or relinquishment; he is without conceptualization in all respects and free from differentiated conceptualization.”

“Mañjuśrī! It is like space, which is equal in all places, without discrimination or differentiated discrimination; it is neither born nor extinguished; it is not of the past, not of the future, and not of the present; it is invisible and beyond conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*); it is formless, unindicatable, and unmanifestable; it is untouchable, unguardable, immeasurable, and transcends all measurement; it is incomparable and free from all metaphors; it has no dwelling place and cannot be grasped; it is beyond the path of visual consciousness and is free from mind, thought, and mental consciousness; it is signless and without letters; it is without sound and without recollection; it is without grasping and without relinquishing; it is unchangeable and unalterable; it is beyond the path of speech, yet dwells in all places and enters into all places.”

Mañjuśrī! Just as sentient beings, because they rely on the earth which has high, low, and middle [elevations], speak of space as having high, low, and middle [elevations], yet that space itself has no high, low, or middle.
“Mañjuśrī! The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha is also like this:
equal toward all things, without discrimination or differentiated discrimination, neither arising nor ceasing, neither of the past nor of the future.”
It does not come from the past, nor does it exist in the present; it is invisible and beyond playfulness; it is formless, cannot be demonstrated, and cannot be expressed;
it is untouchable and cannot be protected; it is immeasurable and transcends all calculation;
it is incomparable and free from all analogies; it has no abode and cannot be grasped—thus it is detached.
The path of eye-consciousness is apart from mind, thought, and mental consciousness; it is signless, without letters, without sound, and without conceptualization;
it is without grasping and without relinquishing; it cannot be turned back and cannot be exchanged;
it is beyond the path of speech, abiding in all places and entering into all places.

Mañjuśrī! Because the minds of sentient beings possess superior, inferior, and middling qualities, they perceive the Tathāgata as having superior, inferior, and middling aspects; yet in reality, the Tathāgata has no superior, inferior, or middling aspects.
Mañjuśrī! The Tathāgata does not harbor such a thought as:

"This sentient being possesses inferior faith, so I shall manifest an inferior form and color; [this one possesses middling faith, so I shall manifest a middling form and color; this one possesses superior faith, so I shall manifest a superior form and color]."
‘For those sentient beings who possess middling faith, I manifest a middling form and color;
for those sentient beings who possess superior faith, I manifest a superior form and color. “Mañjuśrī!
The Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma is also like this. Mañjuśrī!
The Tathāgata does not have such a thought:
"This sentient being possesses inferior faith; for them, I preach the Dharma of the Śrāvakas.
This sentient being possesses middling faith; for them, I preach the Dharma of the Pratyekabuddhas.
This sentient being possesses superior faith; for them, I preach the Mahāyāna Dharma."
"Mañjuśrī! The Tathāgata does not have such a thought as:
'Because this sentient being has faith in giving, I shall preach the dānapāramitā for them;'"
Because these sentient beings have faith in and uphold the precepts, I preach the *śīlapāramitā* for them;
because these sentient beings have faith in patience, I preach the *kṣāntipāramitā* for them;
because these sentient beings have faith in diligence, I preach the *vīryapāramitā* for them.
Because these sentient beings have faith in meditative concentration, I preach the dhyāna-pāramitā for them;
because these sentient beings have faith in wisdom, I preach the prajñā-pāramitā for them.

The Sūtra on the Tathāgata’s Adorned Wisdom Light Entering the Realm of All Buddhas,
