Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmaruci of India during the Northern Wei Dynasty: "Mañjuśrī!
The Tathāgata is called the Dharma-body."
Mañjuśrī! The Tathāgata is unborn and non-arising. Mañjuśrī!
The Tathāgata has no name, no form, no verbal expression, and no mind, thought, or consciousness.
Mañjuśrī! The Tathāgata is without discrimination and is free from discrimination.

“Mañjuśrī! That which is called ‘Tathāgata’ is named the mark of emptiness that is inexhaustible; it is the limit of exhaustion, the limit of reality, the limit of all dharmas in the equality of emptiness, the limit of non-duality, and the limit of the eternally unknowable locus.”
"Mañjuśrī! The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, is in all places without discrimination and free from diverse discrimination; he is neither inferior, nor middling, nor superior."
In this way, Mañjuśrī!
All dharmas are without discrimination and free from discrimination; they are neither inferior, nor middling, nor superior. Why is this?
Because all dharmas are unattainable. Mañjuśrī,
that which is called the unattainability of all dharmas is the equality of all dharmas.
To speak of the equality of all phenomena is to abide in equanimity;
to speak of abiding in equanimity is to be immovable;
to speak of being immovable is for all phenomena to have no point of reliance.
To say that all phenomena have no basis means they abide without mind;
to say they abide without mind means they are unborn;
to say they are unborn means they do not arise.
If one views it in this way, those minds and mental factors will ultimately be non-erroneous;
if the mind is ultimately non-erroneous, that practitioner can attain reality as it is;
if one attains reality as it is, one does not give rise to conceptual proliferation.
If one does not give rise to conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), one does not engage with any phenomena.
If one neither proliferates nor engages, one does not abide in birth or death;
if one does not abide in birth or death, one cannot be moved.
If one cannot be moved, that dharma cannot be contradicted;
if a dharma cannot be contradicted, it accords with all dharmas;
and that which accords with all dharmas cannot be moved within the nature of dharmas (dharmatā).
If one cannot be moved within the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), one attains the dharma of self-nature;
if one attains the dharma of self-nature, there is nothing to be attained. Why is this?
Because all phenomena arise dependent upon causes and conditions.
If all phenomena arise dependent upon causes and conditions, they are eternally unarisen;
if they are eternally unarisen, they are eternally unattainable.
If the permanent cannot be apprehended, one attains the dharma of the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi);
if one attains the dharma of the limit of reality, one does not abide together with any dharmas;
if one does not abide together with any dharmas, one does not abide in common with others.
If one does not dwell together [with conceptual constructs], they neither exist nor do not exist;
if they neither exist nor do not exist, they abide within the realization of the Dharma;
if they abide within the realization of the Dharma, they attain the practice of the Dharma of right mindfulness.
If one attains the practice of the dharma of right mindfulness, there is not a single dharma therein that is not the Buddha-dharma.
Why is this? Because one realizes that all dharmas are empty.
“Mañjuśrī! To awaken to the emptiness of all phenomena is called bodhi.
Bodhi is the awakening to the emptiness of all phenomena; emptiness itself is bodhi.”
Thus, emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, non-action, non-activity, non-reliance, non-arising, non-grasping, and non-abiding—awakening to such dharmas is called bodhi.
"Bodhi is called the cultivation of right mindfulness.
Mañjuśrī! That which is called the cultivation of right mindfulness is neither grasping nor rejecting; this is precisely what is termed right mindfulness."
Non-contemplation and non-differentiation are called practice;
non-attachment, non-binding, and non-liberation are called practice;
non-departure and non-arrival are called practice.
“Mañjuśrī! For one who practices with right mindfulness, there is no practice, no benefit, no fruit, and no realization in that state. Why is this?
Mañjuśrī! Because the intrinsic nature of the mind is pure, that mind is defiled by adventitious afflictions, yet the intrinsically pure mind is not defiled.
That intrinsically pure mind is the very essence; it is neither defiled nor undefiled.
Because there is no counteractive dharma in that state, by what dharma could one counteract and extinguish these afflictions?
Why is this? That purity is not [an attainment of] purity; it is primordial purity itself.
If it is fundamentally pure, it is non-arising;
if it is non-arising, it is unstained;
if it is unstained, it does not depart from the dharma of staining.
If one is free from defiled phenomena, they extinguish all defilements.
By what dharma are all defilements extinguished?
By non-arising.
If there is no arising, that is bodhi.
Bodhi is called equality; equality is called suchness.
“Tathatā (Suchness) is called ‘non-differentiation.
Non-differentiation is called ‘abiding as it truly is’ within all conditioned and unconditioned phenomena. Mañjuśrī!
Tathatā (Suchness) is that which is neither conditioned nor unconditioned; it is the non-dual dharma.
That which is neither conditioned nor unconditioned, being the non-dual dharma, is Tathatā.
Mañjuśrī! That which is called "suchness" (tathatā) is the reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi);
that which is called the "reality-limit" is not different from that.
"Non-different" refers to that future *tathatā*.
To speak of "future *tathatā*" is precisely what is meant by "non-different";
to speak of "non-different" is precisely that *tathatā*.
That which is called "Suchness" (tathatā) is neither permanent nor non-Suchness.
That which is neither permanent nor non-Suchness is neither defiled nor pure.
That which is neither defiled nor pure is neither arising nor ceasing.
That which is called "neither arising nor ceasing" is the equality of nirvāṇa.
That which is called the "equality of nirvāṇa" neither abides in the world nor abides in nirvāṇa.
That which neither abides in the world nor abides in nirvāṇa is neither of the past, nor of the future, nor of the present.
To say that it is neither past, nor future, nor present means that it is neither inferior, nor middling, nor superior;
to say that it is neither inferior, nor middling, nor superior is itself the Tathāgata.
"To speak of the Tathāgata is to speak of one who speaks the truth;
to speak of speaking the truth is to speak of True Suchness (tathatā);
to speak of True Suchness is to speak of reality as it is (yathābhūta)."
That which is called "reality as it is" is termed the "self";
that which is termed the "self" is non-duality;
the meaning of non-duality is precisely bodhi.
Bodhi is called awakening.
Awakening is the wisdom that enters the three gates of liberation;
wisdom is the wisdom that enters into the equality of all phenomena throughout the three periods of time.
Regarding "words and meaning": the meaning is that all phenomena (*dharma*) are without differentiation.
As for "meaning," it is nameless, wordless, and ineffable.
Regarding "words and wisdom": awakening to all phenomena is called wisdom; cognizing all phenomena is called wisdom.

Regarding the meaning of "meaning" (*artha*): it is the knowledge of sentient beings and the knowledge of consciousness. To fully comprehend meaning is itself the Dharma; the Dharma is itself the meaning.

It is the knowledge of meaning, the knowledge of consciousness, the knowledge of fully comprehending meaning, and the knowledge of the Dharma; it is the knowledge of the abiding of the Dharma and the knowledge of the essence of the Dharma. That which is turned according to the Dharma is the meaning that is turned; the turning of oneself is the meaning of equality and non-duality. The meaning of equality and non-duality is itself equality; that which is equal is itself the meaning.

What is called the equality of meaning, consciousness, and wisdom is precisely the wisdom that enters the gate of non-dual dharmas; it is termed the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), not the provisional meaning (*neyārtha*).
What is called equality is itself equality and itself emptiness (*śūnyatā*);
what is called emptiness is itself the equality of the illusory self.
To speak of the equality of the self is to speak of the equality of dharmas;
to speak of the equality of dharmas is to speak of the equality of detachment;
and the equality of detachment is the equality of awakening.
Awakening to equality is itself bodhi.
"Mañjuśrī! To be attached to form is to be attached to the eye;..."
To be attached to what is perceived is to be attached to intrinsic nature;
to be attached to views is to be attached to a self;
to be attached to one's own person is to be attached to the wisdom of the emptiness of intrinsic nature.
One who clings to the contemplation of improper mindfulness clings to the radiance of dharmas, yet contemplates dharmas without attachment;
one who clings to the defilement of indolence clings to realized wisdom, yet maintains firm and resolute diligence.
To know dharmas as they truly are is called attachment;
to be attached to the five hindrances and the factors of enlightenment is called attachment.
To be unattached to the wisdom of unobstructed liberation is because all dharmas are pure by nature and exist through causes and conditions.

"Furthermore, when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva knows, as they truly are, the causes of defilement and purity, yet does not abide within those causes of defilement and purity: to give rise to a sense of self and to give rise to views is called the cause of defilement;

to enter into the selflessness of all phenomena is called the cause of purity. To perceive a self and what belongs to a self is called the cause of defilement; internal tranquility and non-engagement with external objects is called the cause of purity.

Desires, anger, hatred, harm, and discursive thought are called the cause of defilement; while impurity, loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, equanimity, entry into the twelve links of dependent origination, and patience are called the cause of purity."
The four perversions are the cause of defilement, while the four foundations of mindfulness are the cause of purification;
the five hindrances are the cause of defilement, while the five faculties are the cause of purification;
the six sense bases are the cause of defilement, while the six recollections are the cause of purification.
The seven unwholesome factors are causes of defilement, while the seven factors of enlightenment are causes of purification;
the eight wrong paths are causes of defilement, while the eight right paths are causes of purification;
the nine bases of vexation are causes of defilement, while the nine successive attainments are causes of purification.
The ten unwholesome courses of action are the cause of defilement, while the ten wholesome courses of action are the cause of purification;
briefly stated, all unwholesome thoughts are the cause of defilement, and all wholesome thoughts are the cause of purification.

"Regarding what are called the causes of defilement and the causes of purification, all those phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature; they are without self, without person, without life-force, without a soul, without 'mine,' and without an agent."
Like an illusion, it is signless and inwardly tranquil;
that which is inwardly tranquil is itself cessation;
that which is cessation is the purity of intrinsic nature.
That which is naturally pure is unattainable;
that which is unattainable is placeless;
that which is placeless is reality.
Reality is precisely empty space.
Why is this so? Mañjuśrī!
"There is not a single dharma that either arises or ceases.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
“If dharmas are thus, how does the Tathāgata attain bodhi?
The Buddha addressed Mañjuśrī, saying: “Mañjuśrī!”
"Without root and without abiding, the Tathāgata thus attains bodhi. Mañjuśrī said,
"World-Honored One!"
“What is the root?
What is the dwelling?
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
"The view of a self-body is called the root;
unreal conceptualization is called the dwelling.
That awakening is equanimity, and the Tathāgata knows all dharmas as equal; therefore, it is said that the Tathāgata attains awakening without a root and without a dwelling."
“Mañjuśrī! That which is called ‘bodhi’ is termed ‘purity’ and is also termed ‘quiescence. What is purity?
What is tranquility?
Mañjuśrī! It is that the self and what belongs to the self are empty of the eye.
Why is this? Because their intrinsic nature is empty.
In this same way, the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are empty of "I" and "mine."
Why is this? Because its intrinsic nature is empty.
Therefore, one knows that the eye is empty and does not cling to forms; for this reason, it is called "pure."
In this way, knowing the ear is empty and not clinging to sounds is tranquility;
knowing the nose is empty and not clinging to odors is tranquility;
knowing the tongue is empty and not clinging to flavors is tranquility.
To know that the body is empty and not to cling to touch is tranquility;
to know that the mind is empty and not to cling to phenomena is tranquility. Mañjuśrī!
The intrinsic nature of bodhi is pure because its intrinsic nature is pure. Regarding this purity of intrinsic nature:

that which is called the purity of intrinsic nature is unstained like space, equal to space, and its intrinsic nature is identical to space—just as space is, by its very nature, pure from the beginning.
“Mañjuśrī! That which is called ‘awakening’ (bodhi) is neither grasped nor abandoned.
How is it not grasped?
What is meant by "not abandoning"?
To say "not grasping" means not grasping any dharmas; therefore, it is called "not grasping.
To say "not abandoning" means not abandoning any dharmas; therefore, it is called "not abandoning."
Mañjuśrī! The Tathāgata has crossed over the great flood; therefore, he neither grasps nor abandons, and in that suchness, neither this shore nor the other shore is perceived.
The Tathāgata knows that all dharmas are free from this shore and the other shore; therefore, he is called the Tathāgata. "Mañjuśrī!
Bodhi is without marks and without observation."
What is signlessness and non-contemplation? Mañjuśrī!
Not perceiving eye-consciousness is called signlessness; not perceiving forms is called non-contemplation.
Not seeing ear-consciousness is called signlessness; not hearing sounds is called non-contemplation.
Not seeing nose-consciousness is called signlessness; not smelling odors is called non-contemplation.
Not seeing tongue-consciousness is called signlessness; not knowing tastes is called non-contemplation.
Not perceiving body-consciousness is called signlessness; not cognizing tangibles is called non-contemplation.
Not perceiving mind-consciousness is called signlessness; not cognizing mental phenomena is called non-contemplation.
Mañjuśrī! This is the realm of all these noble ones; that is to say, the realm of the three worlds. Mañjuśrī!
What is called "bodhi" is neither past, nor future, nor present; it is the equality of the three periods of time and the purity of the three periods of time. Mañjuśrī!
What is the wisdom of the three periods of time?
It is that the mind does not engage with past phenomena, consciousness does not proceed toward future phenomena, and mindfulness does not abide in present phenomena.
Therefore, the Tathāgata does not dwell in mind, mentation, or consciousness;
because he does not dwell therein, he is without discrimination and free from conceptualization.
Because he is without discrimination and free from conceptualization, he does not perceive future phenomena or present phenomena, and he does not engage in idle proliferation.
“Mañjuśrī! Bodhi is bodiless and unconditioned.
What is meant by ‘bodiless’?
What is the unconditioned? Mañjuśrī!
That which is bodiless is that which is not known by visual consciousness, nor by auditory, olfactory, gustatory, tactile, or mental consciousness.
Mañjuśrī! That which is not known by mind, thought, or consciousness is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
What is called "unconditioned" does not arise, does not abide, and does not cease; therefore, it is said that the three times are pure and unconditioned.
As it is with the knowledge of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), so it is with the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*). Why is this?
That which is called the "essence" (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena is, in fact, essence-less.
Regarding "absence of essence," there are no two words in that regard. "Mañjuśrī!
What is called 'awakening' (bodhi) is termed the trace of non-differentiation."
What is non-differentiation?
What is the footprint? Mañjuśrī!
Signlessness is called non-differentiation; True Suchness is called the footprint.
Non-abiding is called non-differentiation; the Dharma is called the footprint.
Non-distinction is called non-differentiation; the Reality Limit is called the footprint.
Inconceivability is called non-differentiation; immovability is called the footprint.
Emptiness is called non-differentiation; signlessness is called the footprint.
Non-conceptualization is called non-differentiation; wishlessness is called the footprint.
The name "non-seeking" is non-differentiated; the name "sentient beings" is a traceless footprint.
The essence of sentient beings is non-differentiated; the name "empty space" is a traceless footprint.
The name "non-perception" is non-differentiated; the name "non-arising" is a traceless footprint.
Non-extinction is called non-differentiation; the unconditioned is called the footprint.
Non-activity is called non-differentiation; enlightenment is called the footprint.
Quiescence is called non-differentiation; nirvāṇa is called the footprint.
Non-arising is called non-differentiation; awakening is called the footprint. "Mañjuśrī!
Bodhi cannot be attained by means of the body, nor can it be attained by means of the mind."
Why is this? Mañjuśrī! The body is dull and obstructive;
it is without sensation and without mind, like grass, trees, walls, clods of earth, or reflections.
The mind is like an illusion, empty and non-existent; it is unreal and uncreated.
"Mañjuśrī! To awaken to the body and mind as they truly are is called bodhi; this is according to worldly designations, not the ultimate truth."
Why is this? Mañjuśrī!
Bodhi is neither body, nor mind, nor dharma; it is neither real nor unreal, neither true nor untrue; it cannot be described in such a manner.
Mañjuśrī! One cannot speak of bodhi by means of any dharmas. Why is this?
Mañjuśrī! Enlightenment has no abiding place that can be described. Mañjuśrī!
Just as space cannot be said to have a place of abiding, and is unconditioned, without arising and without ceasing;
so too is bodhi, which cannot be said to have a place of abiding, to be unconditioned, or to have arising and ceasing.
Mañjuśrī! For example, regarding all worldly phenomena, if one seeks their reality, it cannot be described. Mañjuśrī!
Bodhi is also like this; although bodhi is described by means of all dharmas, its reality cannot be apprehended.
Why is this? Mañjuśrī!
Within the reality of dharmas, no names or phrases can be found.
Why is this? Because they are neither born nor extinguished.
“Mañjuśrī! That which is called ‘awakening’ (bodhi) is named that which cannot be grasped and cannot be relied upon. Mañjuśrī!”
What is that which cannot be grasped?
What is that which cannot be relied upon? Mañjuśrī!
To know the eye as it truly is—that it cannot be grasped—and not to see forms is called "non-reliance";
to know the ear as it truly is—that it cannot be grasped—and not to hear sounds is called "non-reliance";
to know the nose as it truly is—that it cannot be grasped—and not to smell odors is called "non-reliance."
To know the tongue as truly ungraspable, yet not to perceive tastes, is called "unreliability.
To know the body as truly ungraspable, yet not to sense tangibles, is called "unreliability.
To know the mind as truly ungraspable, yet not to see phenomena, is called "unreliability."
Mañjuśrī! In this way, the Tathāgata neither grasps nor relies; this is called realizing bodhi.
Thus, in realizing bodhi, one does not grasp the eye nor see forms; therefore, one does not abide in visual consciousness.
Not grasping the ear and not hearing sounds, one therefore does not abide in ear-consciousness;
not grasping the nose and not smelling odors, one therefore does not abide in nose-consciousness;
not grasping the tongue and not cognizing tastes, one therefore does not abide in tongue-consciousness.
Not grasping the body and not perceiving touch, one therefore does not abide in body-consciousness;
not grasping the mind and not cognizing phenomena, one therefore does not abide in mind-consciousness.
Mañjuśrī! The Tathāgata does not abide in mind, thought, or consciousness; therefore, he is named Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha. Mañjuśrī!
Sentient beings have four modes of mental abiding; they rely upon these four modes of mental abiding.
What are the four? They are as follows:

sentient beings abide with the mind relying on form (*rūpa*); likewise, they abide with the mind relying on feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and formations (*saṃskāra*). These are the four modes of mental abiding upon which sentient beings rely.
“Mañjuśrī! These four modes of abiding of the mind, the Tathāgata knows as they truly are—neither arising nor ceasing; for this reason, he is called a Buddha. Mañjuśrī!”
What is called "bodhi" is named emptiness.
Mañjuśrī! Just as the emptiness of all phenomena is not different from the emptiness of bodhi, the emptiness of bodhi is precisely the emptiness of all phenomena.
Just as all phenomena are empty, the Tathāgata knows them as they truly are; thus he is called the Awakened One.
"Mañjuśrī! It is not that emptiness knows emptiness."
Mañjuśrī! Emptiness is itself awakening, and awakening is itself emptiness. Mañjuśrī!
In emptiness there is no emptiness, nor is there awakening, nor is there duality.
By what dharma is emptiness constituted?
By what dharma is awakening constituted?
Yet two names are spoken.
Why is this? Mañjuśrī!

All things are non-dual, signless, and without differentiation; they are nameless and formless, transcending mind, intellect, and consciousness; they are neither arising nor ceasing, neither active nor inactive, neither accumulating nor non-accumulating; they are without letters and without sound.
Mañjuśrī! To speak of "emptiness" is called grasping at conceptual proliferation. Mañjuśrī!
In the foremost dharma, no dharma can be apprehended; this is called emptiness. Mañjuśrī!
Just as one speaks of "space, space," yet there is no space that can be named, it is therefore called space.
Mañjuśrī! Emptiness is also like this; it is called "emptiness of emptiness," yet there is no dharma that can be spoken of and named "emptiness.
Entering all dharmas in this manner is called "entering the gateway of all dharmas."
“Mañjuśrī! All phenomena are nameless, yet they are explained by relying on names. Mañjuśrī!”
Just as a name is not in this place, yet is not apart from this place, so too is it spoken of in dependence upon a name.
What dharma? That dharma is not in this place, yet is not apart from this place.
In this way, Mañjuśrī!
The Tathāgata knows all phenomena as they truly are: fundamentally unborn, unarisen, and unceasing; signless; free from mind, mentation, and consciousness; without letters and without sound.
“Mañjuśrī! That which is called bodhi is equal to space.
Space is neither level, nor low, nor high; likewise, bodhi is neither level, nor low, nor high.”
Why is this? Mañjuśrī!
Dharmas have no real existence.
Mañjuśrī! If phenomena have no real existence, how can you speak of their equality as being neither low nor high? Mañjuśrī!
The Tathāgata thus awakens to the equality of all phenomena, which are neither high nor low.
Having awakened in this way, there is not even the slightest phenomenon that is unequal, neither high nor low.
Just as those phenomena abide, so too does one know them through suchness-knowing-as-it-really-is (*yathābhūtajñāna*).
"Mañjuśrī! What is this knowledge of things as they really are?"
Mañjuśrī! One who knows all phenomena as they truly are understands that all phenomena are non-existent, fundamentally neither arising nor ceasing.
Phenomena are originally unarisen; having arisen, they return to cessation.
Those dharmas arise without an agent and without a grasper, and they cease without an agent and without a grasper.
Mañjuśrī! All dharmas arise dependent on causes and conditions and cease without causes and conditions; there is no real path.
Therefore, the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma for those who seek the path of cessation. "Mañjuśrī!
What is called 'bodhi' is termed the footprint of reality as it is."
Mañjuśrī! What is the footprint of reality as it is? Mañjuśrī!
What is called the "trace of reality" is itself bodhi.
Just as with bodhi, form (*rūpa*) is likewise not separate from suchness (*tathatā*);
likewise, feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) are not separate from suchness.
As with awakening, the earth element does not depart from suchness;
water, fire, and wind likewise do not depart from suchness.
As with awakening, so too the eye element, the form element, and the eye-consciousness element do not depart from suchness.
Mañjuśrī! Just as with awakening, the ear element, the sound element, and the ear-consciousness element do not depart from suchness. Mañjuśrī!
The nose element, the odor element, and the nose-consciousness element do not depart from suchness;
the tongue element, the taste element, and the tongue-consciousness element do not depart from suchness;
the body element, the tactile object element, and the body-consciousness element do not depart from suchness.
The mind-element, the dharma-element, and the mind-consciousness-element do not depart from suchness. Mañjuśrī!
That which is called the "dharma of provisional names" among all dharmas refers to the five aggregates, the twelve bases, and the eighteen elements.
The Tathāgata has awakened to those dharmas as they truly are, not through perverted awakening.
Just as those dharmas abide in the past limit, the middle limit, and the future limit, so too does the Tathāgata know the past limit, the middle limit, and the future limit as they truly are.
Just as those dharmas are not born at their prior limit, do not go away at their future limit, and do not abide in the present limit, one knows them as they truly are.
That footprint of dharmas is such that as it is with one dharma, so it is with all dharmas;
as it is with all dharmas, so it is with one dharma.
Mañjuśrī! Furthermore, neither one nor many can be apprehended. Mañjuśrī!
One enters into all phenomena through the gate of "ā" and the gate of "non-ā. Mañjuśrī!
What is the gate of "ā"?
What is the gate of "A"?
Mañjuśrī, that which is called "A" refers to the initial production of all dharmas of the roots of goodness.
"A" (a) means not seeing any phenomena.
"An-a" (an-ā) means that when the mind does not abide, one causes it to abide;
"an-a" also refers to the liberation door of signless samādhi.
The word "a" refers to counting and observing the characteristics of all phenomena;
the word "an-a" is called "transcending measure.
What is meant by "transcending measure"?
This refers to karma without consciousness.
"A" means contemplating conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*);
"an-a" means contemplating unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
“Mañjuśrī! That which is called ‘awakening’ (bodhi) is a dharma that is without outflows (anāsrava) and without grasping (anupādāna). Mañjuśrī!”
What is that which is without outflows and without grasping? Mañjuśrī!
Regarding the term "outflow-free" (anāsrava), it refers to being free from the four outflows. What are these four? They are:
The outflow of desire, the outflow of existence, the outflow of ignorance, and the outflow of views.
Because one does not grasp at these four kinds of outflows, it is called "being far removed from all outflows."
Mañjuśrī! What is non-appropriation?
It refers to being free from the four types of appropriation.
What are the four? They are:
grasping at sensual desire, grasping at views, grasping at a self, and grasping at precepts and observances.
Because of these outflows, sentient beings are darkened by ignorance and moistened by the waters of craving; they mutually depend upon one another, falsely grasping and clinging. "Mañjuśrī!
The Tathāgata knows my fundamental nature as it truly is; because he knows my purity as it truly is, he knows the purity of all sentient beings as it truly is.
What is called "my purity" and "the purity of all sentient beings"—these two are non-dual and without distinction in meaning; they are precisely neither arising nor ceasing.
Mañjuśrī! Regarding that which is neither born nor extinguished, what dharma-sphere is such that it cannot be known by mind, mentation, or consciousness? Mañjuśrī!
In what phenomena are mind, intellect, and consciousness absent?
Within those phenomena there is no conceptualization; it is by conceptualizing what phenomena that one gives rise to improper mindfulness.
Therefore, the bodhisattva gives rise to right mindfulness.
One who gives rise to right mindfulness does not give rise to ignorance;
one who does not give rise to ignorance does not give rise to the twelve links of existence.
That which does not give rise to the twelve links of existence is non-arising;
that which is non-arising is the state;
the state is the definitive meaning.
The definitive meaning is the ultimate truth;
the ultimate truth is the meaning of non-self;
the meaning of non-self is the meaning of the ineffable.
The meaning of that which is ineffable is the meaning of dependent origination;
the meaning of dependent origination is the meaning of phenomena (dharma);
the meaning of phenomena is the meaning of suchness (tathatā).
Therefore, to see dependent origination is to see the Dharma; to see the Dharma is to see the Tathāgata.
As for what is called "seeing," although one sees all phenomena, there is nothing seen.
Mañjuśrī! To say that there is something seen refers to seeing the mind and seeing contemplation.
The Tathāgata does not see the mind.
If one does not perceive the mind and does not perceive contemplation, that is the vision of reality. Mañjuśrī!
All those dharmas are thus equal, and the Tathāgata knows them as equal to those dharmas.
“Mañjuśrī! That which is called ‘awakening’ (bodhi) is termed pure, stainless, and spotless. Mañjuśrī!”
What is purity? What is freedom from defilement?
What is freedom from blemish?
Mañjuśrī! Emptiness is called purity; signlessness is called stainlessness; wishlessness is called being without blemish. Mañjuśrī!
Non-arising is called purity; non-activity is called stainlessness; non-origination is called being without blemish.
Mañjuśrī! Innate nature is called purity; the purity of roots of goodness is called stainlessness; the perfection of radiance is called being without blemish.

The absence of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) is called "pure"; being free from conceptual proliferation is called "stainless"; the cessation of all conceptual proliferation is called "spotless.
Just as the name is pure, the *dharmadhātu* is stainless, and the *bhūtakoṭi* is spotless;
just as space is pure, non-obstruction is stainless, and non-perception is spotless.

Purity within is called "pure"; non-engagement without is called "stainless"; the non-perception of both within and without is called "spotless. The accumulation of the aggregates (*skandha*) is called "pure";
the intrinsic nature of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) is called "stainless"; the twelve sense bases (*āyatana*) being without going is called "spotless.

The knowledge of exhaustion regarding the past is called "pure"; the knowledge of non-arising regarding the future is called "stainless"; the knowledge abiding in the dharma-realm in the present is called "spotless."
Mañjuśrī! To speak briefly, purity, stainlessness, and spotlessness enter into the single track of the equal Dharma, which is called the track of tranquility;
that which is called the track of tranquility is itself cessation.
That which is quiescent is called pure;
that which is pure is the noble. “Mañjuśrī!
As is space, so too is bodhi;
as is bodhi, so too are all phenomena (dharma);
as are all phenomena, so too is the essence of phenomena (dharmatā).
As is the nature of dharmas, so too are sentient beings;
as are sentient beings, so too are lands;
as are lands, so too is nirvana.
Mañjuśrī! The Tathāgata has said:

"All dharmas are equal, like nirvāṇa," because they are ultimately and finally without any dharma to be remedied and are free from all dharmas to be remedied; for they are primordially pure, primordially stainless, and primordially without blemish.

Mañjuśrī! When the Tathāgata thus awakens to all phenomena as they truly are and observes the nature of all sentient beings, he immediately gives rise to a pure, stainless, and unsullied, vigorous mind of great compassion.
“Mañjuśrī! How does a bodhisattva practice the bodhisattva conduct? Mañjuśrī!”

If a bodhisattva does not give rise to such thoughts— neither for the sake of the exhaustion of all phenomena, nor for the sake of the arising of all phenomena, nor for the sake of the non-arising of all phenomena—
and perceives that all phenomena are primordially exhausted, yet perceives that all phenomena are inexhaustible without giving rise to a conceited mind,
saying: "I know it thus."
Yet they do not destroy the fact that all phenomena are originally unborn.
Mañjuśrī, it is in this way that a bodhisattva practices the bodhisattva conduct.
"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī!

A bodhisattva does not perceive a past mind that has ceased while practicing the bodhisattva path; does not perceive a future mind that has not yet arrived while practicing the bodhisattva path; and does not perceive a present mind that exists while practicing the bodhisattva path. Thus, without clinging to the past, future, or present, they practice the bodhisattva path within the mind in this manner."
“Mañjuśrī! A bodhisattva’s giving and that of a Tathāgata are non-dual and without distinction; practicing in this way is called practicing the bodhisattva path.
A bodhisattva’s upholding of the precepts and that of a Tathāgata are non-dual and without distinction; practicing in this way is called practicing the bodhisattva path.”
The bodhisattva of patience and the Tathāgata are non-dual and without distinction; practicing in this way is called practicing the bodhisattva path.
The bodhisattva of diligence and the Tathāgata are non-dual and without distinction; practicing in this way is called practicing the bodhisattva path.
The bodhisattva of meditative concentration and the Tathāgata are non-dual and without distinction; practicing in this way is called practicing the bodhisattva path.
“Mañjuśrī, the bodhisattva and the Tathāgata are non-dual and without distinction; practicing in this way is called practicing the bodhisattva path.”
A bodhisattva does not perceive form as empty, nor does he perceive form as not empty; practicing in this manner is called practicing the bodhisattva path.
Why is this? Because the emptiness of form is the very nature of form.
In this way, Mañjuśrī!

A bodhisattva does not practice with regard to feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, nor does he depart from feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; practicing in this manner is called practicing the bodhisattva path.
Why is this? Because one does not perceive mind, thought, or consciousness. "Mañjuśrī!
There is not a single dharma that is to be known or abandoned, nor one to be cultivated or realized.
Mañjuśrī! As for what is called "exhaustion," those dharmas are eternally exhausted; they are not non-exhausted, for they are exhausted from the very beginning.
If a dharma is fundamentally exhausted, that dharma cannot be exhausted;
because it cannot be exhausted, it is therefore called "exhausted. Why is this?
Because it is exhausted according to reality.
If it is exhausted according to reality, that dharma does not exhaust even a single dharma;
if it does not exhaust even a single dharma, that dharma is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
If a dharma is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), that unconditioned dharma is neither born nor extinguished; this is called the Tathāgata.

Whether a Tathāgata appears in the world or does not appear in the world, the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), the essence of phenomena (*dharmatva*), the stability of phenomena (*dharma-sthiti*), the fixedness of phenomena (*dharma-vyavasthāna*), and the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) remain as they truly are.
The dharma-realm abides as it truly is; the knowledge of dharmas neither arises nor ceases, and by relying on that knowledge, one knows unconditioned dharmas. Mañjuśrī!
If one enters such stations of all dharmas, one knows that all outflowing dharmas neither arise nor cease.

Mañjuśrī! When one speaks of the "exhaustion of all outflows," this is said based on worldly names and conventional designations; yet in that true suchness, the dharma-body, there is no arising of dharmas, nor is there any cessation of dharmas.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī Dharmaputra rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and with palms joined toward the Buddha, praised the Tathāgata with sublime verses,
speaking this hymn: "Without form, without marks, Without faculties, without abode, Because you are neither born nor extinguished,
I pay homage to the One who has nothing to observe."
Neither abiding nor departing, neither grasping nor relinquishing,
because you are far removed from the six sense bases, I pay homage to you who have nothing to observe.
Having transcended the three realms, you are equal to space.
Because you are unstained by any desires, I pay homage to you who have nothing to observe.
Because you remain constantly in tranquility amidst all modes of conduct— whether going, coming, sleeping, or waking—
I pay homage to you who have nothing to observe.
Past and future are entirely equal;
because you abide in equality and do not destroy equality, I pay homage to you who have nothing to observe.
Entering into signless concentrations, you perceive the stillness of all phenomena.
Because you constantly enter into equanimity, I pay homage to you who have nothing to observe.
All Buddhas have the characteristic of space, and space itself has no characteristic;
because you are free from all causes and effects, I pay homage to you who have nothing to observe.
Space has neither center nor periphery, and the bodies of all Buddhas are likewise;
because the mind is identical to space, I pay homage to that which is without an object of observation.
The Buddha always dwells in the world, yet remains unstained by worldly dharmas.
I pay homage to the one who does not conceptualize the world and has nothing to observe.
All phenomena are like illusions, yet the illusion itself cannot be apprehended;
because you are free from all illusory phenomena, I pay homage to the one who has nothing to observe.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Mañjuśrī, saying:
“Excellent, excellent, Mañjuśrī!”
"Speak this Dharma quickly!
Mañjuśrī, it is so, it is so."

The Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, should not be seen by means of form, nor should they be seen by means of dharmas, nor should they be seen by means of marks, nor should they be seen by means of secondary characteristics, nor should they be seen by means of the nature of dharmas.
Mañjuśrī! The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, cannot be seen by individuals alone, nor can they be seen by a multitude. Mañjuśrī!
Of all the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, there is no one who sees them, no one who hears them, no one who makes offerings to them in the present, and no one who will make offerings to them in the future.
Mañjuśrī! The Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, do not say that all phenomena are one, nor do they say that all phenomena are many. Mañjuśrī!
The Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, do not realize bodhi.
The Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, are not named in reliance upon a single dharma, nor are they named in reliance upon many dharmas. Mañjuśrī!
The Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, do not see any dharmas, do not hear any dharmas, do not think of any dharmas, do not know any dharmas, and do not awaken to any dharmas. Mañjuśrī!
The Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, do not speak of a single dharma, nor do they point out any dharmas. Mañjuśrī!
The Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, in the present, do not speak of any dharmas, nor do they point out any dharmas.
Mañjuśrī! The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, neither drink nor eat. Mañjuśrī!
The Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, have no dharma to be realized. Mañjuśrī!
The Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, do not sever defiled dharmas, nor do they realize pure dharmas.
Mañjuśrī! The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, do not see any dharmas, do not hear any dharmas, do not smell any dharmas, and do not cognize any dharmas.
Why is this? Because all dharmas are fundamentally pure. "Mañjuśrī!

If someone were to establish as many sentient beings as there are atoms in a trichiliocosm in the stage of a pratyekabuddha, yet they did not give rise to faith in this Dharma-gate, and if there were another bodhisattva who did have faith in this Dharma-gate, the merit of this latter bodhisattva would still exceed that of the former; how much more so for anyone who, regarding this Dharma-gate, either writes it themselves or causes others to write it?
"Their merit would be greater than that, immeasurable and boundless. Mañjuśrī!
If all sentient beings in the trichiliocosm—whether born from eggs, born from wombs..."
Whether born from moisture or by transformation, whether possessing form or formless,
whether with perception or without perception, whether one-footed, two-footed, three-footed,
four-footed, many-footed, or footless— if all those sentient beings were, for a single moment, to obtain...
Suppose all human beings were to give rise to the bodhicitta and become bodhisattvas; and each of these bodhisattvas were to offer and provide sustenance—
food, drink, clothing, beds, bedding, medicinal decoctions for the sick, various necessities of life,
and every kind of object of pleasure— to as many Buddhas as there are atoms in Buddha-lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Toward all such Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Bodhisattvas, and the community of Śrāvakas,
and so on for as many asaṃkhyeya kalpas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges;

after those Tathāgatas, Bodhisattvas, and Śrāvakas have entered parinirvāṇa, one constructs stūpas made of the seven precious substances, one yojana in height, surrounded on all sides by railings of various jewels, interspersed with garlands of maṇi gems, with precious pillars, banners, and canopies erected, and covered above by nets of sovereign maṇi-jewel kings— the merit obtained thereby is beyond calculation.

Furthermore, if there is a bodhisattva who, with a mind of ultimate purity, believes in this *Tathāgatavyūha-jñānaprabhāsa-sarvabuddhaviṣayāvatāra-sūtra*, believes in this dharma-gate, enters this dharma-gate, does not doubt this dharma-gate, and gives rise to a pure mind toward this dharma-gate—even if they expound a single verse for others—the merit obtained by this bodhisattva will be exceedingly great, immeasurable, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*).

Compared to this merit, the former merit does not equal even one hundredth part; it does not equal one thousandth part (kalā); it does not equal one hundred-thousandth part; it does not equal one ten-millionth part; it does not equal one hundred-thousand-ten-millionth part; it does not equal one hundred-thousand-ten-million-billionth part; it does not equal even a numerical fraction, nor can it be reached by calculation, analogy, or comparison.
Why is this? Because it enables the accomplishment and realization of Buddha-wisdom. "Mañjuśrī!..."

If there is a lay bodhisattva who, with food and drink, clothing, beds and couches, bedding, medicinal decoctions for the sick, various necessities of life, and all manner of articles of pleasure, makes offerings and provides support to as many Tathāgatas, Bodhisattvas, and Saṃghas of Śrāvakas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, and continues to do so for as many asaṃkhyeya kalpas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, the merit obtained would be beyond measure and calculation.

Furthermore, if there is an ordained bodhisattva whose mind is pure in upholding the precepts, and who gives even a single mouthful of food to a single animal, the merit obtained will be exceedingly great, immeasurable, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*).

Compared to this merit, the former merit does not equal even one hundredth part; it does not equal one thousandth part of a *kalā*; it does not equal one ten-millionth part; it does not equal one hundred-thousand-ten-million-billionth part; it does not equal even a small fraction of a *kalā*; indeed, it cannot be reached by calculation or analogy.

“Mañjuśrī! Suppose there were as many renunciant bodhisattvas as there are atoms in a trichiliocosm, all of whom maintain the precepts with pure minds. If each of these bodhisattvas were to offer and provide—through food, drink, clothing, beds, bedding, medicinal decoctions for the sick, various necessities of life, and every kind of article of pleasure—to the Tathāgatas, bodhisattvas, and assemblies of śrāvakas throughout the worlds of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, for as many asaṃkhyeya kalpas as there are sands in the Ganges, the merit they would obtain would be beyond measure.”

Furthermore, if there is a bodhisattva who maintains the precepts with a pure mind—whether a householder or one who has gone forth—who hears this Dharma-gate and gives rise to faith without doubt, and either writes it down themselves or instructs others to write it down, the merit they obtain will be exceedingly great, immeasurable, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*).

Compared to this merit, the merit of the previous bodhisattva’s practice of giving does not equal even one hundredth part, nor one thousandth part (kalā), nor one ten-millionth part, nor even a numerical fraction; it is beyond reach even by calculation or analogy.

“Mañjuśrī! If there were a bodhisattva mahāsattva who, with the seven treasures filling a trichiliocosm, were to offer them as a gift and provide sustenance to all the Buddhas, Tathāgatas, for as many eons as there are atoms in a trichiliocosm, the merit obtained would be beyond measure and calculation.”

Furthermore, if there is a bodhisattva who, for the sake of another bodhisattva, explains even a single four-line verse from within this Dharma-gate, the merit obtained will be exceedingly great, immeasurable, and incalculable (asaṃkhyeya).

Compared to this merit, the former merit does not equal even one hundredth part; it does not equal one thousandth part (kalā); it does not equal one hundred-thousandth part; it does not equal one hundred-thousand-ten-millionth part; it does not equal any numerical fraction; it does not equal even a minute fraction (kalām api); it does not equal any calculable fraction; indeed, it cannot be reached by calculation or analogy.
“Mañjuśrī! Setting aside the merit obtained from giving away the seven treasures that fill a trichiliocosm for as many eons as there are atoms in a trichiliocosm;”

Mañjuśrī! Suppose there were as many bodhisattvas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, and each of these bodhisattvas were to take as many asaṃkhyeya buddha-fields as there are grains of sand in the Ganges and transform them into worlds of Jāmbūnada gold; suppose all the trees therein were wrapped in celestial garments, and they were covered above by nets of *sarva-prabhāsa-rāja* maṇi jewels, with pavilions made of *vaijayanta-rāja* maṇi jewels, railings made of *vidyut-prabha* maṇi jewels, and wish-fulfilling gems filling those worlds; and suppose they erected banners, pennants, and canopies made of every kind of jewel, making offerings and presenting gifts daily to as many Tathāgatas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges for as many asaṃkhyeya kalpas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges—the merit obtained from such giving would be beyond measure and calculation.

Furthermore, if there is a bodhisattva who believes in this Dharma-door and, for the sake of other bodhisattvas, explains even a single four-line verse from within this Dharma-door, the merit obtained will be exceedingly great, immeasurable, and incalculable (asaṃkhyeya).

Compared to this merit, the former merit does not equal even one hundredth part; it does not equal one thousandth part (kalā); it does not equal one hundred-thousand-millionth part; it does not equal one hundred-thousand-billionth part; it does not equal any numerical fraction; it does not equal even a minute fraction (kalām api); it does not equal any portion (saṃkhyām api); it does not equal any calculable fraction; it does not equal even an upaniṣad fraction; indeed, it cannot be reached by calculation, analogy, or comparison.

“Mañjuśrī! Suppose all sentient beings within the three realms were to be pulled out from among the hells, the animal realm, and the realm of hungry ghosts by a lay bodhisattva and established in the stage of a pratyekabuddha; the merit obtained would be beyond measure.”

Furthermore, if there is another renunciant bodhisattva who gives even a single mouthful of food and drink to an animal, the merit obtained will surpass the former merit by immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) amounts.

“Mañjuśrī! Suppose there were ten thousand lands, equal in number to the atoms of incalculable billions of nayutas, hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas, of renunciant bodhisattvas;
and each of these bodhisattvas, throughout the worlds of the ten directions...”
In each and every direction, they see ten billion unspeakable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of atoms of dust worths of Buddhas,
Tathāgatas; and for each and every Tathāgata, as well as for all the Bodhisattvas and the assembly of Śrāvakas,
they provide food and drink, clothing, bedding, seats, and medicinal decoctions for illness and debility, in various kinds [of offerings].
He provided for the livelihood of all beings with a full thousand *koṭi-nayuta*, hundred-thousand *koṭi-nayuta*,
and unspeakably many *nayuta* of worlds filled with every requisite for happiness, including sovereign *maṇi* jewels, bestowing them upon each and every Tathāgata,
along with their Bodhisattvas and Śrāvaka Saṃghas, day by day, continuing in this manner up to a thousand *koṭis*.
The merit obtained over unspeakable eons, as numerous as the atoms within a hundred thousand million billion nayutas of Buddha-lands, is beyond all calculation or description.

Furthermore, if there is a bodhisattva who believes in this dharma-gate and bestows even a single mouthful of food and drink upon a single animal, the merit obtained will be exceedingly great, immeasurable, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*).

Compared to this merit, the former merit does not equal even one hundredth part, nor one thousandth part (kalā), nor one hundred-thousandth part, nor one ten-millionth part, nor one hundred-thousand-ten-millionth part, nor one hundred-thousand-ten-million-billionth part, nor one saṃkhyeya part, nor even a minute fraction (kalām api), nor a numerical part; it cannot be reached even by calculation or analogy.
Why is this? Because they are able to believe in this dharma-gate, which is the seal of the non-retrogressive bodhisattva. "Mañjuśrī!

If there is a bodhisattva who teaches and transforms all sentient beings in all worlds throughout the ten directions, establishing them in the practice of faith; and if there is another bodhisattva who transforms a single sentient being, establishing them in the practice of meaning—the merit obtained by the latter surpasses the former merit immeasurably and boundlessly.

Furthermore, if there is a bodhisattva who teaches and transforms all sentient beings in all worlds throughout the ten directions, establishing them in the practice of meaning (artha-caryā); and if there is another bodhisattva who transforms a single sentient being, establishing them in the practice of the Dharma (dharma-caryā), the merit obtained by the latter surpasses the former merit immeasurably and boundlessly.

“Mañjuśrī! Suppose there were a bodhisattva who taught and transformed all sentient beings in all worlds throughout the ten directions, establishing them in the practice of the Dharma; and suppose there were another bodhisattva who transformed a single sentient being and established them among the eight persons (aṣṭamaka). The merit obtained by the latter would surpass the merit of the former by immeasurable asaṃkhyeya.”

“Mañjuśrī! Suppose there were another bodhisattva who, through teaching and transforming all sentient beings in all worlds throughout the ten directions, established them within the stage of the eight persons; and suppose there were yet another bodhisattva who transformed a single sentient being and caused them to attain the fruit of a srotāpanna. The merit obtained by the latter would surpass the merit of the former by immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas.”

“Mañjuśrī! Suppose there were a bodhisattva who taught and transformed all sentient beings in all worlds throughout the ten directions, causing them to attain the fruit of a srotāpanna; and suppose there were another bodhisattva who transformed a single sentient being, causing them to attain the fruit of a sakṛdāgāmin. The merit obtained by the latter would surpass the merit of the former by immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas.”

“Mañjuśrī! Suppose there were a bodhisattva who taught and transformed all sentient beings in all worlds throughout the ten directions, causing them to attain the fruit of a sakṛdāgāmin; and suppose there were another bodhisattva who transformed a single sentient being, causing them to attain the fruit of an anāgāmin. The merit obtained by the latter would surpass the merit of the former by immeasurable asaṃkhyeya.”

“Mañjuśrī! Suppose there were a bodhisattva who taught and transformed all sentient beings in all worlds throughout the ten directions, causing them to attain the fruit of anāgāmin; and suppose there were another bodhisattva who transformed a single sentient being, causing them to attain the fruit of arhat. The merit obtained by the latter would surpass the merit of the former by even an immeasurable asaṃkhyeya.”

“Mañjuśrī! Suppose there were a bodhisattva who taught and transformed all sentient beings in all worlds throughout the ten directions, causing them to attain the fruit of arhatship; and suppose there were another bodhisattva who transformed a single sentient being, causing them to attain the path of a pratyekabuddha. The merit obtained by the latter would surpass the merit of the former, even to the extent of immeasurable asaṃkhyeyas.”

“Mañjuśrī! If there were another bodhisattva who taught and transformed all sentient beings in all worlds throughout the ten directions, causing them to attain the path of a pratyekabuddha; and if there were yet another bodhisattva who transformed a single sentient being, causing them to resolve upon bodhicitta—the merit obtained by the latter would be immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (asaṃkhyeya).”

“Mañjuśrī! Suppose there were a bodhisattva who taught and transformed all sentient beings in all worlds throughout the ten directions, causing them to resolve upon bodhicitta; and suppose there were another bodhisattva who transformed a single sentient being, causing them to attain the stage of non-retrogression—the merit obtained by the latter would surpass the merit of the former by even an immeasurable asaṃkhyeya.”

“Mañjuśrī! Suppose there were a bodhisattva who taught and transformed all sentient beings in all worlds throughout the ten directions, causing them to attain the stage of non-retrogression; and suppose there were another bodhisattva who, having faith in this Dharma-gate, either wrote it out himself, taught others to write it out, or extensively explained it to others. The merit obtained by the latter would surpass the former merit by an immeasurable asaṃkhyeya, such that even a hundred thousand million nayutas of parts of the former would not equal one part of the latter.”
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
“A bodhisattva is able to uphold The wondrous Dharma of ten billion Buddhas;
Yet if a person hears this sutra, Their merit shall surpass that of the former.”
To pay homage at the feet of all Buddhas, they travel through the ten directions by means of their supernormal powers;
with flowers, incense, and unguents, they make offerings to ten billion Buddhas.
If there are those who hear this sutra and explain it for others even for a brief moment, [they shall attain such merit].
The merit of this surpasses that, its number being immeasurable.
If one hears of the Buddha’s Dharma-body and explains it to a second person,
that dull-witted listener will give rise to sharp wisdom and swiftly realize the unsurpassed path.
For the sake of the Buddha among gods and humans, they construct various wondrous stupas;

numbering in the fulfillment of immeasurable billions, reaching upward to the Summit of Existence and extending all around throughout the ten directions, within these stupas they erect banners and streamers.
With golden bells and canopies of the seven treasures, one thus makes offerings to the Buddha.
If a bodhisattva hears this sutra and is able to write it out themselves,
or teaches others to write it out, their merit shall surpass that [of the former].
If a person upholds this sutra, they will remain far removed from stinginess and envy;
their merit shall be immeasurable, and they will swiftly attain great bodhi.
This sutra reveals the dharmakāya, appearing like various forms manifesting within space.
"Countless Buddhas have spoken [thus]; therefore, you should protect and uphold it.

When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, Mañjuśrī the Dharma Prince, along with immeasurable, asaṃkhyeya, unspeakably unspeakable numbers of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, as well as the assembly of śrāvakas and all the worldlings—devas, humans, asuras, and others—hearing what the Buddha had taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
The Sūtra on the Tathāgata’s Adorned Wisdom-Light Entering the Realm of All Buddhas, Scroll II.
